opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this as a kind of pyramid, because no single data source is going to get us there on its own. Each one has a very different profile of strengths and weaknesses, and the art is in how you combine them.

At the bottom, the widest layer, you have internet-scale data: text, images, and especially video. It's massive and diverse, and it gives you a lot of common sense. It tells you what objects are, how people interact with them, and roughly how the physical world tends to unfold. But it has a fundamental gap: there are no motor actions in it. When you watch a YouTube video of someone cooking, you don't get the joint torques or the control signals. So it's a fantastic prior for the "brain," the vision-language understanding and high-level reasoning, but it doesn't directly teach a robot how to move.

In the middle you have simulation data. I think of simulation as the way you turn compute into data. Real-world data is bounded by how many robots and how many hours you have, and you're stuck with the 24 hours in a day. In simulation you can run thousands of environments in parallel, faster than real time, with randomized physics, lighting, textures, and object shapes. That domain randomization matters: if a policy works across a thousand variations of a simulated world, there's a much better chance the real world just looks like the thousand-and-first variation. The weakness, of course, is the sim-to-real gap. Physics engines aren't perfect, especially for contact-rich manipulation, deformable objects, and fluids. Increasingly I think generative models, video and world models, will complement classical physics simulation here, so you get both the precision of a physics engine and the visual diversity of a neural simulator.

At the top, the smallest but most precious layer, is real robot data, usually collected through teleoperation. It's the ground truth. It has no sim-to-real gap, and it captures all the messy details of real hardware and real environments. But it's extremely expensive and slow to collect. You're paying humans to puppeteer robots, and it doesn't scale the way internet data does. People sometimes call it "burning human fuel."

So the strategy is to use all three for what each is best at. Pretrain on internet-scale data for broad understanding. Scale up with simulation, both physics-based and neural, to get massive amounts of action-labeled experience. Then use real robot data to ground and fine-tune everything so it actually works on physical hardware. And it should be a flywheel: real data helps you build better simulators and world models, those generate more useful synthetic data, and better policies make real-world collection more efficient.

The deeper point is that robotics doesn't have its own internet to scrape, so we have to manufacture our data. Whoever builds the best recipe for mixing these sources, the right ratios and the right way to bridge the gaps between them, will have a big advantage in getting to generalist robots.

r001.rationale: The response says to use all three sources together: internet data for broad understanding, simulation for scalable action-labeled experience, and real robot data to ground and fine-tune the result.

fable-5.1.text:
I think of it as a data pyramid, and the three layers are not interchangeable. They each buy you something different, and the mistake people make is trying to get everything from one layer.

At the base you have internet data. It's enormous, it's basically free, and it's where the robot learns the semantics of the world. What a kitchen looks like, what a mug is for, how humans move their bodies when they open a door. Every video of a person doing a task is a weak demonstration. The problem is that internet data has no actions. Nobody uploads the motor torques along with the YouTube video. So you get world knowledge and common sense, but not control.

The middle layer is simulation. This is where you get action data at scale. Once you have a simulator, you can generate millions of trajectories, with physics, with perfect labels, with randomized lighting and textures and object placements. You can run ten thousand robots in parallel on a single GPU and fast-forward a year of experience in a few hours. That's how we trained things like dexterous hands and humanoid locomotion. Simulation is where the robot learns to actually move. The weakness is the sim-to-real gap. The physics is approximate, contact is hard, deformable objects are hard, and the visuals, even with good rendering, are never quite the real world.

At the top, the smallest and most expensive layer, is real robot data. Teleoperation, real deployments, a human in a VR headset puppeteering the robot. This is the ground truth. It captures everything simulation gets wrong. But it's slow and it doesn't scale. You can't fast-forward real time, and every hour of data costs you a human operator and a robot that might break.

So the strategy is to use each layer for what it's good at. Internet data gives you the priors, a foundation model that understands scenes and language and human motion. Simulation gives you the bulk of the action experience and the diversity. Real data is the alignment step, the small amount of high-quality signal that closes the gap and corrects the simulator's mistakes. Think of it the way language models work: massive pretraining, then a much smaller fine-tuning phase on carefully curated data.

And the layers should feed back into each other. Real data tells you where your simulator is wrong, so you fix the simulator. Internet video, especially human video, can be retargeted into the simulator as motion priors. And the whole thing gets more valuable as the foundation model gets better, because a model that already understands the world needs far fewer real-world samples to learn a new skill.

The teams that will win are the ones that treat this as one pipeline rather than three separate camps arguing about which data source is the right one.

r001.rationale: The response assigns complementary roles to internet, simulation, and real robot data, then says they should work together as one feedback pipeline.

astra-6.text:
I think of them as complementary sources of experience. Internet data gives you breadth: what objects are, how people describe tasks, and what everyday activities look like. But watching a video of someone picking up a cup doesn’t necessarily teach a robot how much force to apply or what to do when the cup slips.

Simulation gives you a place to practice. You can run many environments in parallel, vary the objects and physics, and let the robot fail without breaking hardware. The challenge is that a policy can get very good at your simulator while still missing something important about the real world.

Real robot data grounds the whole process. It exposes the friction, contact dynamics, sensor noise, and other details that your simulation doesn’t capture. It’s expensive, so you want to use it strategically—both to improve the policy and to identify where the simulator needs to get better.

So I’d build a loop: learn broad representations from the internet, develop and stress-test skills in simulation, then use real-world experience to correct the gaps. The key is making those sources reinforce each other, rather than expecting any one of them to solve robotics on its own.

r001.rationale: It describes a loop that learns from internet data, develops skills in simulation, and uses real-world experience to correct gaps, with all three sources reinforcing each other.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of them as three complementary sources of experience. Internet data gives you breadth: objects, language, human activities, and a lot of common sense about the world. But watching a video of someone picking up a cup doesn’t automatically tell a robot what forces to apply or how to recover when the cup slips.

Simulation lets you turn that broad knowledge into practice. You can run many robots in parallel, vary the objects and environments, and give them experience with failures that would be slow or expensive to collect in the real world. The challenge is that a policy can learn to exploit the simulator, so success there isn’t the final test.

Real robot data grounds the whole process. It exposes the contact dynamics, sensing errors, and other details your simulation missed. You use those failures to improve the policy and decide what to simulate next.

So I wouldn’t frame it as choosing one data source. The strategy is a loop: learn broadly from the internet, practice at scale in simulation, and use real-world experience to keep that learning honest.

r001.rationale: It presents internet, simulation, and real robot data as complementary sources in a single learning loop for a robotics strategy.
